newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU wins more powers in investigating mergers.
newsitem.headline: EU wins more powers in investigating mergers.

text.p: European Union industry ministers agreed on Thursday to increase the role of the European Commission in determining whether mergers and takeovers are in line with the bloc's competition rules.

The EU executive's authority to vet such deals will be extended to include mergers which do not now reach required turnover thresholds if they would otherwise need to be notified nationally in at least three member states.
This means that more corporate transactions will qualify for the fast-track, one-stop shop clearance procedure of the European Commission, further increasing its workload.

The agreed amendment to the EU's merger regulation was designed to reduce problems with "multiple national filings" where companies planning to merge need the approval of several national competition authorities.
The European Commission says this increases uncertainty, efforts and costs for businesses.
"We have taken an important step to make life easier for industry," said Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers, who chaired the meeting.

EU Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert, welcoming the agreement, estimated that it would initially result in the Commission reviewing 10 more cases per year compared with a total of around 125 mergers or takeovers last year.
But he told a news conference the number was expected to increase because of more mergers in the EU's single market.
The ministers agreed on the compromise deal put forward by the Dutch EU presidency after Britain dropped its reservations.

The outcome represented a second best solution for the European Commission, which had orginally proposed a straightforward lowering of the turnover thresholds to give it more say in vetting mergers in the 15-nation EU.
However, this had been rejected by several member states, wary of handing over too much powers in the sensitive competition field to Brussels.

Under present rules, the EU executive automatically vets mergers if the global turnover of the companies involved is at least five billion European currency units ($5.7 billion) and their EU turnover reaches 250 million Ecus or more for each company.

Under Thursday's agreement a deal requiring three or more national filings would instead fall under the EU's merger regulation if the firms' combined turnover is more than 2.5 billion Ecus and if their total turnover is at least 100 million Ecus in each of three member states.

In addition, the turnover of each of at least two of the firms involved must be more than 25 million Ecus in each of the three member states. The EU-wide turnover of at least two of the companies should also be more than 100 million Ecus.
Britain had originally proposed to reduce the worldwide turnover only to three billion Ecus.

Van Miert has long argued that a lowering of the thresholds would be beneficial for industry as more corporate deals would only need the approval of one body rather than of several national competition authorities.
He also says several deals in expanding businesses such as media and pharmaceuticals have EU-wide implications even if they do not now reach current turnover limits.
They should therefore be reviewed by the Commission's competition officials.
The EU executive already has wide powers in the competition field, including the possibility to block mergers and takeovers. ($ = 0.881 European Currency Unit ECUs)
